newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU says already promoting human rights in Cuba.
newsitem.headline: EU says already promoting human rights in Cuba.

text.p: The European Union said on Thursday it was already pushing for greater human rights in Cuba after the United States suggested such action could defuse a bitter row over a U.S. law targeting foreign investment in Cuba.

"We are involved...in trying to make democracy happen in Cuba," EU president Jacques Santer told journalists at a dinner. "But we do not believe that this democratization process can occur by the use of embargos...and isolation."
The United States indicated earlier on Thursday that planned lawsuits against European companies doing business in Cuba could be dropped if its EU allies visibly promoted Cuban human rights.

The U.S. law, which has sparked a united show of opposition from EU members, gives Cuban-Americans the right to sue foreign companies that own or operate properties seized by the Cuban government from exiles after the 1959 communist revolution.

Visiting Denmark, President Bill Clinton's special envoy Stuart Eizenstat said cooperation from European allies in "elevating the human rights issue" could make it easier for the president to shelve implementation of the so-called Helms-Burton law, already delayed since July.

"The president, in order to continue the suspension of those suits, has to make the finding that a further suspension would be in the security interest of the country and would expedite the transition to democracy in Cuba," he said.
"That's why we look to our European friends...to elevate the human rights issue so the president will be in a position -- if he wishes -- to consider to exercise that waiver," he said.
Santer said the law had been "universally condemned" and that the United States should not be using its "super-power strength" in such a way.
He said it would be shame for the dispute to "substantially overshadow" otherwise excellent relations between the EU and the United States and that it was urgent to end the quarrel.
The law, tightening the U.S. embargo against the Caribbean island, was passed after Cuba shot down two U.S. light planes in February, alleging that they had strayed into U.S. airspace.
An EU countermeasure agreed earlier this week will prohibit European individuals or companies from complying with the act and allowing them to reclaim damages in EU courts.
Canada and Mexico have also passed retaliatory legislation.
